edges.effect_quant: Among 454 women referred for heavy menstrual bleeding, 42.8% had ferritin below 15 microg/L and 72.5% were below 30 microg/L; in a Swedish von Willebrand cohort with heavy menstrual bleeding, 45% had ferritin below 30 microg/L.
edges.population: adolescents and reproductive-age women with heavy menstrual bleeding
edges.mechanism: Repeated excessive menstrual blood loss depletes iron faster than ordinary dietary intake can replace it, gradually lowering ferritin and eventually hemoglobin. The risk rises further when bleeding is prolonged, untreated, or compounded by bleeding disorders.
edges.summary: Heavy menstrual bleeding is strongly linked to iron deficiency in both adolescent and adult gynecology cohorts, with low ferritin and overt anemia common in referred populations. The signal is clinically important and consistent, even though exact prevalence depends on referral severity and whether an underlying bleeding disorder is present.
edges.caveats: Most estimates come from specialty clinics, so community prevalence may be lower than in referral cohorts. Nonetheless, the direction is robust enough that routine iron assessment is well justified when heavy menstrual bleeding is present.
